newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria floats idea of oil refinery privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria floats idea of oil refinery privatisation.

text.p: Africa's oil giant Nigeria has floated the idea of privatising or contracting out management of its problem-plagued refineries.

"NNPC (Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation) despatched a letter to oil companies asking whether they would be interested in participating in part or total privatisation of oil refineries, and if they are they should feel free to discuss it with us," state-run NNPC spokesman Edem Duke told Reuters on Tuesday.
"It has not gone beyond an exploratory level, there has been no discussion of a time-frame and no discussion of modalities," he added.

Despite pumping over two million barrels of crude oil per day Nigeria has frequently had to resort to fuel imports because of technical problems at its four refineries which never come close to running at their full capacity of 445,000 barrels per day (bpd).
In September after a series of repairs the four were running at about 230,000 bpd.
NNPC managing director Dahiru Bayero has estimated the cost of bringing the refineries up to capacity at about $859 million.
Oil marketing companies welcome the possibility of greater private sector involvement in the downstream sector, but warn that it would only work if government freed up subsidised prices.
"There is clearly a large domestic market as well as regional potential," said one oil marketing company executive.
"I could certainly see involvement on the management side, but to get anyone else to invest money would be unlikely unless they are sold outright at a very low price and pricing margins are changed."
NNPC receives only 1.70 naira ($0.021) per litre for refining and distribution, which the World Bank says should cost at least twice as much.
The price at the petrol pump is 11 naira ($0.138) per litre, with 1.30 naira ($0.016) going to marketing companies, whose profits are derived largely from sales of grease, oil and other chemicals.
The World Bank has recommended outright sale of Nigeria's refineries as the only long-term solution.
"Leasing run-down facilities requires prior rehabilitation investments whereas divestment can bring in the necessary capital financing in exchange for a lower sale price," a recent report said.

The group leader of the Bank's oil and gas division, Eric Daffern told a conference in South Africa on Monday that Nigeria's refineries were among the few on the continent that could prove profitable.
He said that one of them "more or less was" but the others were not.

Industry analysts say that if Nigerian refineries were properly managed it would be a blow to Ivory Coast's refinery, which uses Nigerian crude to supply the West and Central African market and which plans to expand capacity.

In Nigeria the New Plant at the southeastern Port Harcourt refinery has a capacity of 150,000 bpd and the Old Plant 60,000 bpd. Southern Warri can run at up to 125,000 bpd and Northern Kaduna at 110,000 bpd. ($1=80 naira)
